1135.title: the Shiva Sahasranama (selections)
1135.hook: Vishnu offers Shiva a lotus for every name, and at the last name, the lotus is gone
1135.howItsDone: Hindus tell this story of Vishnu's lotuses in the Shiva Purana, and in a Shiva temple a devotee may sponsor an archana in which a flower is offered at each of Shiva's names.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Last time, the Shiva Sahasranama brought Pashupati, lord of every creature, the one who loosens the rope. A new week, and a new story.
screen: `PASHUPATI LOOSENS THE ROPE.` · `A NEW WEEK, A NEW STORY.`

segments.voice: One lotus is missing. Vishnu has been kneeling before Shiva for a long time, saying a name and laying down a lotus, a name and a lotus, over and over. There should be a flower for every name. Now, with one name left to say, his hand reaches into the basket and finds nothing. That's how the Shiva Purana tells it, and it's how that Purana frames its own list of Shiva's names.
screen: `A NAME, A LOTUS.` → `ONE NAME LEFT.` → `THE BASKET IS EMPTY.`

segments.voice: In the Shiva Purana, Vishnu needs Shiva's help. The demons are winning, so Vishnu goes to Shiva's shrine to honor him with a thousand names, a lotus at each one. Shiva decides to test him, and quietly hides one lotus. So: the empty basket. What does Vishnu do? He could stop and call the worship good enough. He could leave and come back with more flowers. Instead he remembers what people call him: Kamala-nayana, the lotus-eyed. His eyes are lotuses, he thinks, so he means to offer one of them. As he reaches to take out his own eye, Shiva appears and stops him, delighted, and gives him a gift: the Sudarshana, the blazing discus Vishnu carries in his hand from then on. The story does a few things at once. It makes the hymn of Shiva's names part of how Vishnu received his discus. It holds two great gods, often worshipped by different communities, together in one scene of devotion, with no one shamed. And it says something about what the names are for. Vishnu wasn't reciting a list to get to the end of it. Every name was a real offering, and when the offering ran short, he gave what he had. The last name mattered as much as the first. That's the hard part of any long practice: the last name, the last rep, the last page, said like it still counts.
screen: `VISHNU: A NAME AND A LOTUS EACH.` · `SHIVA HIDES ONE LOTUS.` · `THE LOTUS-EYED OFFERS HIS EYE.` · `THE SUDARSHANA, A GIFT.`

segments.voice: On each in-breath, gather something small to offer, a person you're grateful for, a moment from today, a plain thank you, and on each out-breath, lay it down, the latest as real as the first. When your attention wanders, that's your empty basket: just come back, and give the next breath. If you pray, you can offer each breath to Shiva, or to God.
The Shiva Sahasranama. Today's selection: the Shiva Purana's story of Vishnu offering a lotus at every name, and his own eye when one went missing.

1136.title: the Shiva Sahasranama (selections)
1136.hook: Nilakantha, the blue-throated: the name Shiva earned by swallowing what nobody else would touch
1136.howItsDone: Hindus tell the churning of the ocean in the Mahabharata and the Puranas, and devotees honor Shiva as Nilakantha, the blue-throated one, in hymns, images and temples bearing that name.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Shiva Sahasranama, Vishnu laid a lotus at every name, and offered his own eye when one went missing. Today, a name with a scar.
screen: `A LOTUS AT EVERY NAME.` · `A NAME WITH A SCAR.`

segments.voice: In paintings and posters of Shiva, look at his throat. It's blue. Not his whole body, though he's often painted pale or ash-gray or blue all over. The throat carries a darker stain, like a bruise. Some of his names describe how he looks or what he rules. This one remembers something he did, and marks the place on his body where it happened: Nilakantha, the blue-throated one.
screen: `LOOK AT HIS THROAT.` → `A NAME THAT REMEMBERS.` → `NILAKANTHA.`

segments.voice: Nila is blue, a dark blue-black, and kantha is the throat. The story behind it is the churning of the ocean, told in the Mahabharata and the Puranas. The gods and the demons want amrita, the nectar of immortality, and it lies at the bottom of the ocean of milk. So they make a churn out of a mountain, use the great serpent as the rope, and pull, the gods at one end and the demons at the other. Wonderful things rise out of the waves, but something terrible too: a poison, halahala, so strong it begins to burn the worlds. Nobody wants it. The gods and the demons both turn to Shiva. And Shiva drinks it. Here the tellings add a tender detail. In some, Parvati puts her hand to his throat so the poison won't go down any further. In others his own power holds it there. Either way, the poison stops at the throat and stains it blue. He keeps the world safe by keeping the poison where it can't destroy him or anyone else. So the name is a scar, worn openly. It doesn't say Shiva is untouched by poison. It says he held it. Some readers reach for this story when someone in a family or workplace takes in a hard thing so it doesn't spread: the bad news, the angry call, the blame. Not swallowing it so it eats you from inside. Not spitting it back at the room. Holding it at the throat, and letting it stop there.
screen: `NILA, KANTHA: BLUE, THROAT.` · `THE CHURNING OF THE OCEAN.` · `SHIVA DRINKS THE POISON.` · `HELD AT THE THROAT, NOT SWALLOWED.`

segments.voice: Swallow once, then let the breath move slowly through the throat, cool on the way in, warm on the way out. Let one hard thing from this week come to mind, a sharp word you heard or one you almost said, and without pushing it down or sending it out, let it rest at the throat for a breath or two and lose some of its heat. If you pray, you can say Nilakantha softly.
The Shiva Sahasranama. Today's name from it: Nilakantha, the blue-throated, who drank the poison from the churning ocean and held it at his throat.

1137.title: the Shiva Sahasranama (selections)
1137.hook: Kapardin, the one with braided hair: a Vedic poet's word for the wild god he asks to keep a village well
1137.howItsDone: Images of Shiva show his coiled, matted hair with the crescent moon and the Ganga, and the Rig Veda's hymns to Rudra, which call him kapardin, are still chanted in Vedic recitation.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday the Shiva Sahasranama gave Nilakantha: the blue throat that held the poison. Today, the braided hair.
screen: `NILAKANTHA, THE BLUE THROAT.` · `THE BRAIDED HAIR.`

segments.voice: A prayer for a village can be very practical. Keep the children well. Keep the animals healthy. Let nobody fall sick. In the Rig Veda, a poet brings exactly that kind of prayer to Rudra, the fierce god whose names Shiva carries. And before he asks for anything, he names him: strong, and kapardin, the one with braided, coiled hair. Not his weapon. Not his throne. His hair.
screen: `A PRAYER FOR A VILLAGE.` → `NOT A WEAPON. HIS HAIR.` → `KAPARDIN.`

segments.voice: Tradition reads kaparda as a braid or coil of hair, and kapardin as the one who wears it. The poet brings his songs to Rudra, the strong, the braided-haired, and says what they're for: that it may go well with the two-footed and the four-footed, that everyone in this village may thrive, free of sickness. Health, for people and animals, in one small place. Now notice who he's asking. In the hymns, Rudra is a god of the wild places, the mountain and the edge of things. And later tradition reads coiled, uncut hair as the mark of someone who lives outside the household, with no barber and no hearth. So a village, with its children and its cattle, turns to the one who doesn't live in it, and asks him to keep it well. The name doesn't tame the hair. It doesn't comb it or cut it. It keeps it. Kapardin is among the names in the sahasranama, and images of Shiva keep the piled, coiled locks, with a crescent moon tucked in, and the river from the Nataraja days. Some readers hear a plain lesson in the old verse about where help comes from. Not always from the center of things. Sometimes from the edge: the one who lives apart, who doesn't keep the village's hours, and who is still asked, by name, to look after it. The poet's wish stays practical to the end: a village where nobody is sick.
screen: `KAPARDA: COILED, MATTED HAIR.` · `A VILLAGE ASKS FOR WELL-BEING.` · `THE WILD ONE, ASKED FOR HELP.` · `THE NAME KEEPS THE OLD WORD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the place you live, your building, your block, your village, and on each in-breath call up one home in it, or one person you pass there, even someone you've never spoken to. On each out-breath, wish them well, health today and nobody in that house sick, moving from door to door without needing their names. If you pray, you can offer the wish to Shiva as Kapardin, or to God.
The Shiva Sahasranama. Today's name from it: Kapardin, the one with coiled, braided hair, a Vedic poet's word for the wild god he asked to keep a village well.

1138.title: the Shiva Sahasranama (selections)
1138.hook: a poor boy who wanted milk becomes the sage who hands Krishna the names, and the names are gathered up as Mahadeva
1138.howItsDone: Devotees of Shiva address him as Mahadeva in daily speech and worship, and some recite his sahasranama in full on Mondays or on Maha Shivaratri, offering something at each name.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday the Shiva Sahasranama gave Kapardin, the braided-haired wild god a Vedic poet asked to keep a village well. Today, the last selection.
screen: `KAPARDIN, THE BRAIDED HAIR.` · `THE LAST SELECTION.`

segments.voice: A little boy wants milk. He's seen another child drink it, and he asks his mother. They're poor, living in a forest hermitage, and there's no milk to give. So she stirs some flour into water and hands it to him. He drinks it, and knows it isn't milk. That small kitchen moment is where the Mahabharata begins the story of Upamanyu, the sage who handed Krishna Shiva's names.
screen: `A BOY ASKS FOR MILK.` → `FLOUR IN WATER.` → `WHERE THE NAMES CAME FROM.`

segments.voice: In the Mahabharata, Upamanyu tells Krishna his own story. When the boy cries over the flour and water, his mother tells him they have nothing, and that only Shiva can give what he's asking for. So the boy sets out to worship Shiva, with his whole small life, in hard austerities. One day a visitor arrives: Indra, king of the gods, riding his white elephant, offering the boy any gift he wants. Upamanyu turns him down. He wants nothing that doesn't come from Shiva. Then the visitor changes. It was Shiva all along, testing him, and now Shiva shows himself, with Parvati beside him, and gives the boy far more than milk. That's who Krishna is sitting with when he hears the names: someone who asked for one thing and was given the god himself. When Upamanyu has taught him, Krishna worships Shiva, and Shiva and Parvati appear to him too, and grant his wish for a son. Across these selections, a handful of names: Sthanu, the post. Shankara and Shambhu, the makers of well-being. Pashupati, who loosens the rope. Nilakantha, the blue throat. Kapardin, the wild one a village asks for help. And Vishnu's lotuses, an offering at every name. One more name gathers them up: Mahadeva, the great god. Not great like a king who keeps his distance. Great like the one who turned up at a poor boy's hermitage, and answered him. The list is long because the god is large. But the story at its root is small: a child, a cup, an honest no to everything else.
screen: `UPAMANYU REFUSES INDRA'S GIFTS.` · `SHIVA REVEALS HIMSELF.` · `KRISHNA RECEIVES HIS WISH.` · `MAHADEVA GATHERS THE NAMES.`

segments.voice: Let the names you've met pass through your mind, one per breath, like beads on a string: Sthanu, steady; Shankara, well-being; Pashupati, the loosened rope; Nilakantha, the held poison; Kapardin, the village kept well; Mahadeva. Notice which one you linger on; that's the one that's yours for now. If you pray, you can say that name a few times, slowly.

1139.title: Kashmir Shaivism opening (the Shiva Sutras)
1139.hook: a teacher dreams of words cut into a rock, and the first of them says consciousness is the self
1139.howItsDone: In the Kashmir Shaiva tradition the Shiva Sutras are studied with a teacher and a commentary, such as Kshemaraja's, one short line at a time.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shiva Sahasranama closed with Mahadeva, and the boy who wanted milk. Today, a new book opens.
screen: `MAHADEVA GATHERS THE NAMES.` · `A NEW BOOK OPENS.`

segments.voice: A rock on a mountainside in Kashmir. That's where this story says a teaching was waiting. Tradition remembers a teacher named Vasugupta, a devotee of Shiva, who had a dream. In it, Shiva told him that on a certain mountain there was a great stone, and on the stone, words were cut: short lines of teaching that had been forgotten. Vasugupta woke up. And now he has to decide what a dream is worth.
screen: `A ROCK IN KASHMIR.` → `VASUGUPTA'S DREAM.` → `THE SHIVA SUTRAS.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Vasugupta went. He climbed to the place from the dream, found the stone and touched it, and it turned over, showing the lines carved underneath. Some commentators tell it differently: Shiva taught him in the dream itself. Either way, the tradition treats the Shiva Sutras as given, not invented. This is the opening of Kashmir Shaivism. A sutra is a thread, a line so short a teacher has to unpack it. And the very first thread of this book is two words: chaitanyam atma. Consciousness is the self. Sit with how strange and how simple that is. It doesn't say you have consciousness, the way you have a phone or a cold. It says you are it. Not the body, not the name, not the job title, not the mood you woke up in. Those come and go. The awareness that notices them coming and going: that's the self. And Kashmir Shaivism takes one more step. That consciousness isn't a small private light in each head. It's Shiva's own, one consciousness, appearing as everything and everyone. So the first line of the book is also a line about God. Commentators in this tradition, like Kshemaraja, linger over these two words, and read the rest of the book as unfolding from them. The sahasranama gave Shiva a long string of names, each one a door. Here the tradition goes the other way: no long list, just one thread, pointing not out at Shiva but in, at whoever is listening.
screen: `THE STONE TURNS OVER.` · `SUTRA: A THREAD TO UNPACK.` · `CHAITANYAM ATMA.` · `ONE CONSCIOUSNESS, SHIVA'S OWN.` · then, large: `CONSCIOUSNESS IS THE SELF.`

segments.voice: Let sounds come in, a car, a fan, your own breathing, and thoughts too, and each time something appears, say softly to yourself: noticed. Every so often, turn around and ask what is doing the noticing, and without answering in words, rest in whatever is aware for a breath or two. If you pray, you can hold the first sutra, consciousness is the self, as your line.

1140.title: Kashmir Shaivism opening (the Shiva Sutras)
1140.hook: the second thread of the Shiva Sutras says knowledge is bondage, and means the small, limited kind
1140.howItsDone: Students of Kashmir Shaivism read the Shiva Sutras slowly with a commentary, and the tradition's teachers describe freedom as recognition (pratyabhijna) of one's own nature as Shiva.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FORTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kashmir Shaivism opening: a rock turned over, and the first thread of the Shiva Sutras said consciousness is the self. Today, the second thread.
screen: `CONSCIOUSNESS IS THE SELF.` · `THE SECOND THREAD.`

segments.voice: Knowledge is bondage. That's the whole second line of the Shiva Sutras, two words in Sanskrit: jnanam bandhah. Read it cold and it sounds like an attack on school, on books, on curiosity, on everything a library stands for. It isn't. But it's meant to stop you, the way a do-not-enter sign makes you look twice at the door. The first thread said consciousness is the self. This one says what goes wrong.
screen: `KNOWLEDGE IS BONDAGE.` → `NOT AN ATTACK ON BOOKS.` → `WHAT GOES WRONG.`

segments.voice: Consciousness is the self, and in this tradition that consciousness is Shiva's own: wide, free, whole. So if that's what a person is, why can life feel so cramped? The second thread answers: knowing binds. Commentators in the tradition read knowledge here as a particular kind of knowing: limited knowing. The quiet, constant sense of I am only this. Only this body. Only this anxious person with this bank balance and this argument from last week. Not wrong information, but too small a picture of who's doing the knowing. That small picture is the knot. It isn't a punishment, and in this teaching it isn't a sin. It's closer to a habit of seeing. Look at a vast sky through a keyhole long enough, and you start to think the sky is keyhole-shaped. The commentators notice something gentler underneath. If bondage is a kind of knowing, then freedom is a kind of knowing too. Not a new fact. A recognition: the same consciousness, seeing itself without the keyhole. One school in Kashmir takes its name from this idea, pratyabhijna, recognition: nothing has to be built from scratch, only seen again. On an ordinary day, the small knowing sounds like I'm just not a patient person, or I'm the one who always messes up. Labels that started as information and became walls. The second thread doesn't ask you to stop knowing things. It asks who you think is doing the knowing.
screen: `JNANAM BANDHAH: KNOWING BINDS.` · `LIMITED KNOWING: I AM ONLY THIS.` · `A SKY SEEN THROUGH A KEYHOLE.` · `FREEDOM AS RECOGNITION.`

segments.voice: Let a sentence come up that starts with I'm just, or I'm only, or I always, something you say about yourself, and hold it gently. On each out-breath, let the space around it grow wider, the way the view opens when you step back from a keyhole and open the door; the label can stay, it just isn't the whole room anymore. If you pray, you can rest in the first thread, consciousness is the self.

1141.title: Kashmir Shaivism opening (the Shiva Sutras)
1141.hook: a thread of the Shiva Sutras says wonder marks the stages of yoga, and the week ends on astonishment
1141.howItsDone: Students of Kashmir Shaivism read the Shiva Sutras with a teacher and a commentary, and the tradition describes wonder, vismaya, as a sign of the yogi's progress.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FORTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kashmir Shaivism opening gave the second thread: knowledge is bondage, the small knowing that says I am only this. Today, a thread of wonder.
screen: `KNOWING BINDS.` · `A THREAD OF WONDER.`

segments.voice: A toddler sees a dog. Not for the first time, not even close, and still the whole body lights up: the pointing finger, the gasp, the word shouted at the whole street. Dog! Somewhere along the way, grown-ups stop gasping at dogs. The Shiva Sutras, a book of very short, very serious lines about the self and Shiva, has a thread that sounds like that toddler wrote it. Vismayo yogabhumikah. Wonder marks the stages of yoga.
screen: `A TODDLER SEES A DOG.` → `VISMAYO YOGABHUMIKAH.` → `WONDER MARKS THE WAY.`

segments.voice: Vismaya is wonder, astonishment, the wide-eyed surprise of seeing something as if for the first time. And yogabhumikah: the grounds, the levels, the stages of yoga. Put them together and the thread says that in this path, wonder is how you can tell you're on the way. Not a fixed posture, not a list of achievements. Amazement. Why would that be? Go back to the first two threads. Consciousness is the self. And knowing binds: the small sense of I am only this. Commentators in the tradition describe the yogi who starts to see through that small picture. Every time the wider self shows up, the response is astonishment. Not pride. Not I've earned this. Something more like: oh. This was here the whole time? Wonder is what recognition feels like from the inside. So here's the week, in a line. Vishnu offered a lotus at every name, and nearly his eye. Shiva, the blue-throated, held the poison, and Kapardin, the wild one, was asked to keep a village well. The names were gathered as Mahadeva, through a boy who wanted milk. Then the book changed. A rock turned over in Kashmir. Consciousness is the self. Knowing binds. And now: wonder marks the way. Two very different books, and the week ends on a small word that fits both: oh.
screen: `VISMAYA: WONDER, ASTONISHMENT.` · `WONDER MARKS THE STAGES OF YOGA.` · `RECOGNITION FEELS LIKE OH.` · `THIS WEEK: NAMES, THEN THREADS.`

segments.voice: Choose something right in front of you, your hand, a cup, the light on a wall, and look at it the way the toddler looks at the dog: its color, its edges, the fact that it's here at all; when the mind says it's just a cup, look again. Then turn the same wonder inward, on the plain fact that you're aware of anything. If you pray, you can let that wonder be your prayer.
Kashmir Shaivism opening. A thread from the Shiva Sutras: vismayo yogabhumikah, wonder marks the stages of yoga. Astonishment is what recognition feels like.
